authors: Argenziano G, Soyer HP, Chimenti S et al.
title: Dermoscopy of pigmented skin lesions: results of a consensus meeting via the Internet.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Consensus Net Meeting: experts scored dermoscopic images online. Interobserver agreement was fair to good for whole algorithms but poor for most individual dermoscopic criteria. Pattern analysis performed best (positive likelihood ratio 5.1), and agreement on management decisions was kappa 0.53. Kappa is chance-corrected agreement, where 0 means chance level and 1 means perfect.

authors: Nast A, Griffiths CE, Hay R et al.
title: The 2016 International League of Dermatological Societies' revised glossary for the description of cutaneous lesions.
takeaway: Revised ILDS glossary for describing skin lesions (morphology = shape/colour/arrangement vocabulary), set by Delphi voting among national societies: 13 basic terms plus >100 additional descriptive terms; 46 then 34 societies voted in two rounds. It is the reference vocabulary for primary lesions (macule, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, etc.).

authors: Kittler H, Marghoob AA, Argenziano G et al.
title: Standardization of terminology in dermoscopy/dermatoscopy: Results of the third consensus conference of the International Society of Dermoscopy.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Third International Dermoscopy Society (IDS) consensus. It accepts both 'metaphoric' terms (e.g. 'spoke-wheel', 'chrysalis') and 'descriptive' terms (geometry-based: lines, dots, clods, circles), requires definitions for metaphoric terms, discourages new metaphors, and provides a dictionary that maps the two. Most terms published after 2003 were unknown to most participants.

authors: Friedman RJ, Rigel DS, Kopf AW
title: Early detection of malignant melanoma: the role of physician examination and self-examination of the skin.
journal: CA: a cancer journal for clinicians
takeaway: The original ABCD mnemonic paper (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variegation, Diameter >6 mm) for gross inspection, proposed alongside physician and self-examination for finding thin melanomas early. The abstract gives no accuracy data.

authors: MacKie RM
title: Clinical recognition of early invasive malignant melanoma.
takeaway: MacKie's clinical 7-point checklist (later called the Glasgow checklist): major criteria are change in size, shape and colour; minor criteria are diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing and sensation. PubMed holds no abstract, so no accuracy figures are reported here.

authors: Nachbar F, Stolz W, Merkle T et al.
title: The ABCD rule of dermatoscopy. High prospective value in the diagnosis of doubtful melanocytic skin lesions.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Validated Stolz's dermoscopic ABCD rule. The total dermoscopy score (TDS) weights Asymmetry, Border, Colours and Differential structures. Diagnostic accuracy for melanoma was 80.0% with the rule versus 64.4% by naked eye, with NPV 95.8% and PPV 85.3%. Mean TDS was 6.79 for melanoma and 4.27 for nevi.

authors: Menzies SW, Ingvar C, Crotty KA et al.
title: Frequency and morphologic characteristics of invasive melanomas lacking specific surface microscopic features.
takeaway: Menzies method. A lesion is classified as melanoma only if it lacks both negative features (symmetry of pattern, single colour) and has at least one of nine positive features. The model gave 92% sensitivity and 71% specificity for invasive melanoma. 'Featureless' melanomas were missed, so patient history of change is still essential.

authors: Argenziano G, Fabbrocini G, Carli P et al.
title: Epiluminescence microscopy for the diagnosis of doubtful melanocytic skin lesions. Comparison of the ABCD rule of dermatoscopy and a new 7-point checklist based on pattern analysis.
takeaway: Introduced the dermoscopic 7-point checklist. Three major criteria (atypical network, blue-white veil, atypical vascular pattern) score 2 each and four minor criteria score 1 each. Sensitivity/specificity were 95%/75% for the 7-point checklist, 85%/66% for the ABCD rule and 91%/90% for pattern analysis. Less experienced observers did better with the 7-point checklist.

authors: Grob JJ, Bonerandi JJ
title: The 'ugly duckling' sign: identification of the common characteristics of nevi in an individual as a basis for melanoma screening.
takeaway: Origin of the 'ugly duckling' sign: a nevus that looks unlike the patient's other nevi is suspicious. This makes the patient's own nevi the reference for comparison (intra-patient comparison) instead of fixed thresholds. PubMed holds no abstract.

authors: Abbasi NR, Shaw HM, Rigel DS et al.
title: Early diagnosis of cutaneous melanoma: revisiting the ABCD criteria.
takeaway: Reviewed the ABCD criteria. It found no support for lowering the 6 mm diameter cut-off and recommended adding E for 'evolving' (change in size, shape, symptoms, surface or colour), which gives ABCDE.

authors: Soyer HP, Argenziano G, Zalaudek I et al.
title: Three-point checklist of dermoscopy. A new screening method for early detection of melanoma.
takeaway: Three-point checklist (asymmetry, atypical network, blue-white structures) for non-experts. Non-experts reached 96.3% sensitivity but only 32.8% specificity. The expert's overall diagnosis gave 89.6% sensitivity and 94.2% specificity.

authors: Henning JS, Dusza SW, Wang SQ et al.
title: The CASH (color, architecture, symmetry, and homogeneity) algorithm for dermoscopy.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: CASH algorithm (Colour, Architecture, Symmetry, Homogeneity). A total CASH score ≥8 gave 98% sensitivity and 68% specificity for melanoma. This was a single-evaluator pilot, and inter-observer reliability was not tested.

authors: Walter FM, Prevost AT, Vasconcelos J et al.
title: Using the 7-point checklist as a diagnostic aid for pigmented skin lesions in general practice: a diagnostic validation study.
journal: The British journal of general practice : the journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners
takeaway: Validated the original and weighted 7-point checklist (7PCL) in UK general practice. With the weighted 7PCL cut-off raised from 3 to 4, sensitivity was 91.7% and specificity 53.4% for melanoma. For clinically significant lesions, sensitivity was 73.3%, specificity 57.1%, PPV 24.1% and NPV 92.0%.

authors: Gaudy-Marqueste C, Wazaefi Y, Bruneu Y et al.
title: Ugly Duckling Sign as a Major Factor of Efficiency in Melanoma Detection.
takeaway: Nine dermatologists rated 2089 nevus images from 80 patients. Agreement on which nevus was the ugly duckling was moderate (mean pairwise agreement 0.53 on clinical images, 0.50 on dermoscopic images). Specificity was 0.96 with intra-patient comparison versus 0.88 with lesion-focused analysis, and combining both cut the number of nevi flagged for biopsy 6.9-fold.

authors: Olsen EA, Abernethy ML, Kulp-Shorten C et al.
title: A double-blind, vehicle-controlled study evaluating masoprocol cream in the treatment of actinic keratoses on the head and neck.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Masoprocol trial that is the commonly cited source of the 'Olsen' clinical AK grade (I = palpable but barely visible, II = moderately thick, III = very thick/hyperkeratotic). The grading scheme does not appear in the abstract, which reports only lesion counts. The attribution is the conventional one and should be checked against the full text.

authors: Menzies SW, Westerhoff K, Rabinovitz H et al.
title: Surface microscopy of pigmented basal cell carcinoma.
takeaway: Pigmented BCC model: no pigment network, plus at least one of large blue-grey ovoid nests, multiple blue-grey globules, leaf-like areas, spoke-wheel areas, ulceration, or arborizing (tree-like) vessels. On an independent test set, sensitivity was 97% and specificity 92-93%.

authors: Rosendahl C, Tschandl P, Cameron A et al.
title: Diagnostic accuracy of dermatoscopy for melanocytic and nonmelanocytic pigmented lesions.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Primary-care skin cancer series that introduced the 'chaos and clues' approach (a short pattern-analysis algorithm: is the pattern chaotic, then look for clues to malignancy). At 80% specificity, sensitivity was 82.6% with dermatoscopy and 70.5% without. Sensitivity was 98.6% for BCC, 86.5% for pigmented SCC and 79.3% for melanoma, and lichen planus-like keratosis was the most common false positive. The authors note verification bias (only some lesions get histology).

authors: Bourne P, Rosendahl C, Keir J et al.
title: BLINCK-A diagnostic algorithm for skin cancer diagnosis combining clinical features with dermatoscopy findings.
takeaway: BLINCK algorithm (Benign, Lonely/ugly duckling, Irregular, Nervous/patient concern, Change, Known clues). Four primary-care practitioners read 50 lesions. BLINCK had the highest melanoma sensitivity but led to more biopsies, and its overall accuracy was similar to Menzies and clinical assessment.

authors: Zalaudek I, Giacomel J, Schmid K et al.
title: Dermatoscopy of facial actinic keratosis, intraepidermal carcinoma, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma: a progression model.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Dermoscopic progression model for facial actinic keratosis (AK), through intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen disease), to invasive SCC. Red pseudonetwork points to AK; dotted/glomerular vessels and yellow scale point to Bowen disease; hairpin or linear-irregular vessels, white structureless areas, central keratin and ulceration point to invasive SCC. Sensitivity and specificity were not assessed.

authors: Rogers T, Marino ML, Dusza SW et al.
title: A Clinical Aid for Detecting Skin Cancer: The Triage Amalgamated Dermoscopic Algorithm (TADA).
journal: Journal of the American Board of Family Medicine : JABFM
takeaway: TADA (Triage Amalgamated Dermoscopic Algorithm) asks: is the lesion clearly benign (angioma, dermatofibroma, seborrheic keratosis)? If not, look for architectural disorder, starburst pattern, blue-black/grey, shiny white structures, ulceration, or atypical vessels. Across 120 participants, 43% of them without dermoscopy training, sensitivity was 94.8% and specificity 72.3% for skin malignancy.

authors: Vestergaard ME, Macaskill P, Holt PE et al.
title: Dermoscopy compared with naked eye examination for the diagnosis of primary melanoma: a meta-analysis of studies performed in a clinical setting.
takeaway: Prospective in-clinic studies: dermoscopy versus naked-eye examination for melanoma gave a relative diagnostic odds ratio of 15.6 (95% CI 2.9-83.7), or 9.0 after removing two outlier studies.

authors: Carrera C, Marchetti MA, Dusza SW et al.
title: Validity and Reliability of Dermoscopic Criteria Used to Differentiate Nevi From Melanoma: A Web-Based International Dermoscopy Society Study.
takeaway: International web study revalidating dermoscopic melanoma criteria. Interobserver agreement for most individual criteria was poor (ICC ~0.40-0.46; ICC is the intraclass correlation coefficient, an agreement measure for ratings). Six algorithms had similar AUCs. Menzies had the highest sensitivity (95.1%) but specificity of only 24.8%, and ABCD the highest specificity (59.4%).

authors: Dinnes J, Deeks JJ, Grainge MJ et al.
title: Visual inspection for diagnosing cutaneous melanoma in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: Visual inspection for melanoma. In-person diagnosis was much more accurate than image-based diagnosis (relative diagnostic odds ratio 8.54). For in-person assessment at the excision decision, sensitivity was 76.7% and specificity 95.7%. Published algorithms such as ABCD or the 7-point checklist did not clearly improve accuracy, and the evidence was poorly reported.

authors: Dinnes J, Deeks JJ, Chuchu N et al.
title: Dermoscopy, with and without visual inspection, for diagnosing melanoma in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: Dermoscopy plus visual inspection versus visual inspection alone for melanoma, in person: relative diagnostic odds ratio 4.7. At fixed 80% specificity, sensitivity was 92% versus 76%. Formal algorithms are most useful for training and less expert users, and primary-care evidence is limited.

authors: Dinnes J, Deeks JJ, Chuchu N et al.
title: Visual inspection and dermoscopy, alone or in combination, for diagnosing keratinocyte skin cancers in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: Keratinocyte cancers. For BCC, dermoscopy plus visual inspection beat visual inspection alone (relative diagnostic odds ratio 8.2). At 80% specificity, sensitivity was 93% versus 79%; at 80% sensitivity, specificity was 99% versus 77%. There were too few data on cSCC and no evidence supporting formal algorithms.

authors: Chuchu N, Dinnes J, Takwoingi Y et al.
title: Teledermatology for diagnosing skin cancer in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: Teledermatology (remote image-based assessment). For classifying lesions as malignant from photographs, summary sensitivity was 94.9% and specificity 84.3%, with a very wide CI on specificity (48.5-96.8%). Remote assessment tends to over-recommend excision or referral. The evidence base for triage is weak.

authors: Chuchu N, Takwoingi Y, Dinnes J et al.
title: Smartphone applications for triaging adults with skin lesions that are suspicious for melanoma.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: Smartphone apps for suspected melanoma. Sensitivity of the AI-based apps ranged from 7% to 73%. A store-and-forward app with dermatologist review had 98% sensitivity and 30% specificity. Up to 18% of images were 'unevaluable'. Studies were of low quality and no app could be recommended.

authors: Freeman K, Dinnes J, Chuchu N et al.
title: Algorithm based smartphone apps to assess risk of skin cancer in adults: systematic review of diagnostic accuracy studies.
takeaway: Algorithm-based smartphone apps. SkinVision showed 80% sensitivity and 78% specificity for malignant or premalignant lesions in two studies (n=252). The apps cannot be relied on to detect all melanomas, real-world performance is likely worse, and CE marking was judged inadequate protection.

authors: Salinas MP, Sepúlveda J, Hidalgo L et al.
title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of artificial intelligence versus clinicians for skin cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: AI versus clinicians for skin cancer diagnosis. AI sensitivity/specificity were 87.0%/77.1% versus 79.8%/73.6% for clinicians overall. Against generalists the gap was larger (AI 92.5%/66.5% vs 64.6%/72.8%). Against expert dermatologists performance was comparable (86.3%/78.4% vs 84.2%/74.4%). The authors call for real-world AI-assistance studies.

authors: Ware OR, Dawson JE, Shinohara MM et al.
title: Racial limitations of fitzpatrick skin type.
takeaway: Survey of dermatologists and trainees. Fitzpatrick skin type (FST) was built to predict sunburn propensity under phototherapy, but clinicians commonly use it as a proxy for constitutive skin colour or race/ethnicity. The authors urge education on its original intent.

authors: Adelekun A, Onyekaba G, Lipoff JB
title: Skin color in dermatology textbooks: An updated evaluation and analysis.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: Updated audit of skin tone representation in dermatology textbook images. It is the standard citation for under-representation of dark skin in teaching atlases. The research letter has no PubMed abstract, so no percentages are reported here.

authors: Daneshjou R, Vodrahalli K, Novoa RA et al.
title: Disparities in dermatology AI performance on a diverse, curated clinical image set.
takeaway: Diverse Dermatology Images (DDI) dataset: pathology-confirmed images across skin tones. State-of-the-art AI models, and dermatologists themselves, performed worse on dark skin tones and uncommon diseases. Fine-tuning on DDI closed the gap for the models.

authors: Enechukwu NA, Behera B, Ding DD et al.
title: Dermoscopy of Cutaneous Neoplasms in Skin of Color - A Systematic review by the International Dermoscopy Society "Imaging in Skin of Color" Task Force.
takeaway: IDS systematic review of dermoscopy of neoplasms in skin of colour: 1724 instances across many tumour types. Evidence was mostly level V (case reports and series), and phototypes V-VI were under-represented (most data came from phototype IV).

authors: Fernandez JM, Poling KL, Desai AD et al.
title: Primary cutaneous melanoma in Black patients: An analysis of 2464 cases from the National Cancer Database 2004-2018.
takeaway: 2464 melanomas in Black patients from the US National Cancer Database. The lower extremities were the most common site, acral lentiginous melanoma the most common specific subtype (20.3%), and 41.8% presented at stage III or IV. This illustrates that ABCD-style truncal-nevus heuristics translate poorly.

authors: Weir VR, Li Y, Gillis MC et al.
title: Evaluating skin tone scales for dermatologic dataset labeling: a prospective-comparative study.
takeaway: Compared Fitzpatrick, Monk Skin Tone (MST) and other scales against colorimetry (objective colour measurement) for labelling dermoscopic datasets. MST was repeatable and captured differences in AI melanoma scores better than FST. Colour values extracted from dermoscopic images correlated poorly with colorimetry. FST is not a skin-tone proxy.

authors: Mehta H, Sarkar R
title: The Monk skin tone scale: A tool dermatology should not overlook.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: JAAD commentary arguing that dermatology should adopt the 10-point Monk Skin Tone scale, which comes from computer-vision fairness work, for describing skin tone. PubMed holds no abstract.

authors: Pryor Y, He J, Kang J et al.
title: Optical limits in skin reflectance measurement: Quantifying melanin-dependent constraints on erythema detection.
takeaway: Analysed >15,000 spectra from the International Skin Spectra Archive. Melanin systematically masks the haemoglobin signal, which lowers the sensitivity of visible-range erythema (redness) detection in darker skin. The authors frame this as a physics constraint on any visible-light sensor, not only a rater bias.

authors: Kittler H, Guitera P, Riedl E et al.
title: Identification of clinically featureless incipient melanoma using sequential dermoscopy imaging.
takeaway: Sequential digital dermoscopy imaging (SDDI) detects 'featureless' incipient melanomas through change over time. 61.8% of melanomas found at 1.5-4.5 months of follow-up had no specific dermoscopic features. Melanomas tended to enlarge asymmetrically with structural or colour change, while nevi enlarged symmetrically. Changes over <4.5 months were not discriminative.

authors: Salerni G, Terán T, Puig S et al.
title: Meta-analysis of digital dermoscopy follow-up of melanocytic skin lesions: a study on behalf of the International Dermoscopy Society.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
takeaway: Digital dermoscopy follow-up across 5787 patients and 52,739 monitored lesions. 8.3% of lesions were excised, and the number needed to monitor (lesions monitored per melanoma found) averaged 348. One additional melanoma was found per extra month of monitoring, with a higher share of in-situ and thin melanomas.

authors: Swetter SM, Tsao H, Bichakjian CK et al.
title: Guidelines of care for the management of primary cutaneous melanoma.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
takeaway: AAD guideline of care for primary cutaneous melanoma, covering biopsy, histopathology reporting, surgical margins, SLNB and follow-up. It remains the current AAD primary-melanoma guideline as far as this search found (no 2025-26 replacement indexed in PubMed).

authors: Kandolf L, Peris K, Malvehy J et al.
title: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline for diagnosis, treatment and prevention of actinic keratoses, epithelial UV-induced dysplasia and field cancerization on behalf of European Association of Dermato-Oncology, European Dermatology Forum, European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology and Union of Medical Specialists (Union Européenne des Médecins Spécialistes).
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
takeaway: European AK guideline (2024). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by dermatoscopy or RCM/OCT. Biopsy is indicated for suspicious or treatment-refractory lesions, and multiple AKs call for field-cancerization treatment.

authors: Soyer HP, Jayasinghe D, Rodriguez-Acevedo AJ et al.
title: 3D Total-Body Photography in Patients at High Risk for Melanoma: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
takeaway: High-risk patients randomised to added 3D total-body photography plus SDDI via teledermatology, versus usual care. The intervention increased excisions and biopsies (2.01 vs 1.39 per person) and keratinocyte cancers detected. The intervention arm had a lower melanoma rate per person at 1 year (0.08 vs 0.16), which was not significant.

authors: Garbe C, Amaral T, Peris K et al.
title: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline for melanoma. Part 1: Diagnostics - Update 2024.
takeaway: European melanoma diagnostics guideline, update 2024 (valid to end of 2026). It recommends dermatoscopy for clinical diagnosis and stage-based imaging and follow-up, including structured surveillance for second primaries. The abstract emphasises staging.

authors: Stratigos AJ, Dessinioti C, Garbe C et al.
title: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline for invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Part 1: Diagnostics and prevention - Update 2026.
takeaway: 2026 update of the European cSCC diagnostics/prevention guideline. Low-risk versus higher-risk cSCC is defined by risk of recurrence or metastasis, and a new five-group 'difficult-to-treat' cSCC classification is proposed.

authors: Forsea AM, Pampena R, Akay BN et al.
title: International Dermoscopy Society consensus recommendations for the management of lentigo maligna.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
takeaway: 53-expert IDS consensus on lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ on sun-damaged skin). Dermoscopy and RCM support diagnosis, biopsy targeting, delineation of lesion margins and monitoring. Multiple partial biopsies are recommended, blind destructive treatment should be avoided, and margin-controlled surgery is preferred for large or ill-defined lesions.

authors: CHARDON A, CRETOIS I, HOURSEAU C
title: Skin colour typology and suntanning pathways
takeaway: Original paper introducing the individual typology angle (ITA), a colorimetric (CIELAB L*, b*) skin-colour classification linked to tanning behaviour; foundational for objective skin-tone measurement (content from metadata; ITA definition corroborated by Lipnick 2026).

authors: Lui H, Zhao J, McLean D et al.
title: Real-time Raman spectroscopy for in vivo skin cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Real-time in-vivo Raman spectroscopy (vibrational molecular fingerprint, <1 s per lesion) on 518 lesions: ROC AUC 0.879 cancer/precancer vs benign, 0.823 melanoma vs non-melanoma pigmented, 0.898 melanoma vs SK; specificity only 15-54% at 95-99% sensitivity.

authors: Kupetsky EA, Ferris LK
title: The diagnostic evaluation of MelaFind multi-spectral objective computer vision system.
takeaway: Review of MelaFind, an FDA-approved multispectral computer-vision device giving an objective biopsy recommendation; strengths are high sensitivity and objectivity, limits include modest specificity and out-of-pocket cost.

authors: Malvehy J, Hauschild A, Curiel-Lewandrowski C et al.
title: Clinical performance of the Nevisense system in cutaneous melanoma detection: an international, multicentre, prospective and blinded clinical trial on efficacy and safety.
takeaway: Nevisense electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS: measures tissue bioelectric impedance across frequencies) on 1943 evaluable lesions incl. 265 melanomas: sensitivity 96.6%, specificity 34.4%, PPV 21.1%, NPV 98.2%. High-sensitivity/low-specificity rule-out profile.

authors: Dinnes J, Deeks JJ, Saleh D et al.
title: Reflectance confocal microscopy for diagnosing cutaneous melanoma in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: RCM (reflectance confocal microscopy: in-vivo cellular-resolution horizontal optical sections) for melanoma: Pellacani score >=3 sensitivity 92% (95% CI 87-95) vs dermoscopy 72% in pooled analysis; in equivocal lesions specificity 86% RCM vs 49% dermoscopy, sparing ~296 excisions per 1000 at 20% prevalence. Evidence base small; prospective real-world confirmation requested.

authors: Ferrante di Ruffano L, Dinnes J, Deeks JJ et al.
title: Optical coherence tomography for diagnosing skin cancer in adults.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
takeaway: OCT (optical coherence tomography: near-infrared interferometric cross-sectional imaging to ~1-2 mm depth) for BCC: in a hypothetical 1000 lesions at 60% prevalence, OCT misses 31 BCCs (53 fewer than visual+dermoscopy) and yields 93 false positives. Insufficient data for melanoma or cSCC.

authors: Hosking AM, Coakley BJ, Chang D et al.
title: Hyperspectral imaging in automated digital dermoscopy screening for melanoma.
takeaway: 21-wavelength (350-950 nm) hyperspectral dermoscope (mAID) with ML 'Q-score' on dermatologist-selected biopsy lesions: sensitivity 100%, specificity 36%. Small preselected sample; needs larger trials.

authors: Pellacani G, Farnetani F, Ciardo S et al.
title: Effect of Reflectance Confocal Microscopy for Suspect Lesions on Diagnostic Accuracy in Melanoma: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
takeaway: 3165-participant RCT at referral centres: adjunctive RCM raised PPV for melanoma (18.9 -> 33.3) and reduced number-needed-to-excise by 43.4% (5.3 -> 3.0); all 15 delayed melanomas were <0.5 mm thick. NCT04789421.

authors: Cinotti E, Brunetti T, Cartocci A et al.
title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Line-Field Confocal Optical Coherence Tomography for the Diagnosis of Skin Carcinomas.
takeaway: LC-OCT (line-field confocal OCT: combines OCT depth with confocal cellular resolution, vertical/horizontal/3D) vs dermoscopy for malignant tumours (79 BCC, 22 SCC, 10 melanoma): specificity 0.87 vs 0.73 (p=0.013), sensitivity 0.95 for both; gain driven by BCC discrimination.

authors: Cerminara SE, Cheng P, Kostner L et al.
title: Diagnostic performance of augmented intelligence with 2D and 3D total body photography and convolutional neural networks in a high-risk population for melanoma under real-world conditions: A new era of skin cancer screening?
takeaway: 3D total body photography (Vectra WB360) CNN vs 2D-TBP CNN vs dermatologists: 3D-CNN sensitivity 90.0%, specificity 64.6%, AUC 0.92; dermatologists 90%/92.3%; 2D-CNN 70%/40%, AUC 0.68. 3D repeatability R=0.89 vs 0.79; automated naevus counts badly inflated (469 and 1324 vs 210 true).

authors: Primiero CA, Betz-Stablein B, Ascott N et al.
title: A protocol for annotation of total body photography for machine learning to analyze skin phenotype and lesion classification.
takeaway: Protocol for annotating 3D total-body photography for ML: DICOM-labelled metadata, privacy masking, two-step lesion labelling, extraction of skin phenotype (constitutive/facultative colour, naevus distribution, UV damage) and planned public TBP challenge dataset. Relevant to population-scale quantitative skin phenotyping.

authors: Manolakos D, Patrick G, Geisse JK et al.
title: Use of an elastic-scattering spectroscopy and artificial intelligence device in the assessment of lesions suggestive of skin cancer: A comparative effectiveness study.
takeaway: Elastic scattering spectroscopy (ESS; DermaSensor) + AI on lesions suspicious for skin cancer at 4 US sites: overall sensitivity 97.04% (melanoma 96.67%, BCC 97.22%, SCC 97.01%), specificity 26.22%, NPV 89.58%, PPV 57.54%; no significant difference vs dermatologists.

authors: Venkatesh KP, Kadakia KT, Gilbert S
title: Learnings from the first AI-enabled skin cancer device for primary care authorized by FDA.
takeaway: Analysis of the 2024 FDA authorization of DermaSensor as the first AI-enabled skin cancer device for non-specialists (primary care), discussing its clinical evidence and the regulatory precedent it sets for AI/ML dermatology devices.

authors: Mtimet L, Boussingault L, Aktas D et al.
title: Line-field confocal optical coherence tomography of basal cell carcinoma: A retrospective study on diagnostic performance.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
takeaway: 303 lesions (173 BCC): LC-OCT increased accuracy for BCC vs imitators by 24% over clinical exam and 12% over dermoscopy, and similar gains for superficial-BCC subtype discrimination; 'millefeuille' lobule pattern is a key feature. Proposed algorithm needs validation.

authors: Sellyn GE, Lopez AA, Ghosh S et al.
title: High-frequency ultrasound accuracy in preoperative cutaneous melanoma assessment: A meta-analysis.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
takeaway: HFUS (high-frequency ultrasound) for preoperative melanoma thickness vs histologic Breslow depth: mean correlation 0.87 at 10-20 MHz, 0.94 at 20-25 MHz, 0.98 at >=70 MHz; more accurate for melanomas >0.75 mm; 86% of 36 studies omitted key lesion-depth metrics.

authors: Lipnick MS, Chen D, Law T et al.
title: Comparison of methods for characterizing skin pigment diversity in research cohorts.
takeaway: Compared ITA (individual typology angle = arctan((L*-50)/b*), from CIELAB colorimetry) with Fitzpatrick, Monk Skin Tone and Von Luschan scales and self-reported race (33,856 assessments): 'dark' prevalence ranged 7-26% by method; ITA and L* agreed across two devices (rho>0.7); published ITA cut-offs for dark skin are too light, under-representing dark skin.

authors: Katragadda C, Finnane A, Soyer HP et al.
title: Technique Standards for Skin Lesion Imaging: A Delphi Consensus Statement.
takeaway: ISIC Delphi consensus (Katragadda 2017): 33 skin-imaging recommendations covering lighting, background, field of view, orientation, focus, resolution, scale, colour calibration and storage. Foundation of ISIC imaging standards.

authors: Finnane A, Curiel-Lewandrowski C, Wimberley G et al.
title: Proposed Technical Guidelines for the Acquisition of Clinical Images of Skin-Related Conditions.
takeaway: Companion paper showing ISIC imaging standards are feasible in practice: clinical photographers produced exemplar regional, close-up and dermoscopic images following each recommendation (lighting, scale, colour calibration, etc.).

authors: Caffery LJ, Clunie D, Curiel-Lewandrowski C et al.
title: Transforming Dermatologic Imaging for the Digital Era: Metadata and Standards.
takeaway: Compares consumer image formats with DICOM (the radiology imaging/metadata standard) for dermatology; DICOM carries patient, study and technical metadata and enables interoperability, enterprise imaging and image-retention compliance. Basis of the DICOM dermatology working group effort.

authors: Codella NCF, Gutman D, Celebi ME et al.
title: Skin lesion analysis toward melanoma detection: A challenge at the 2017 International symposium on biomedical imaging (ISBI), hosted by the international skin imaging collaboration (ISIC)
journal: 2018 IEEE 15th International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI 2018)
takeaway: ISIC challenge at ISBI 2017 defining public benchmark tasks (lesion segmentation, dermoscopic feature detection, disease classification) that standardized evaluation across the field (task details from title/metadata only).

authors: Celebi ME, Codella N, Halpern A
title: Dermoscopy Image Analysis: Overview and Future Directions.
journal: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
takeaway: Overview of dermoscopy image analysis organized around segmentation, feature extraction (hand-crafted colour/shape/texture) and classification; notes the field accelerated after the 2016 ISIC public dataset, open-source CNN tooling and cheap GPUs.

authors: Eapen BR, Kaliyadan F, Ashique KT
title: DICODerma: A Practical Approach for Metadata Management of Images in Dermatology.
takeaway: DICODerma: open-source tooling to tag, search and convert dermatology clinical images to DICOM and integrate them with enterprise imaging, aimed at lowering the barrier to standards adoption.

authors: Mirikharaji Z, Abhishek K, Bissoto A et al.
title: A survey on deep learning for skin lesion segmentation.
takeaway: Survey of 177 deep-learning skin lesion segmentation papers covering datasets, architectures, losses, annotation requirements and evaluation metrics; artefacts (hair, bubbles), lesion contrast and acquisition variability remain key challenges.

authors: Esteva A, Kuprel B, Novoa RA et al.
title: Dermatologist-level classification of skin cancer with deep neural networks.
takeaway: Landmark Nature paper: CNN trained on 129,450 clinical images (2,032 diseases) performed on par with 21 board-certified dermatologists on biopsy-proven keratinocyte carcinoma vs SK and melanoma vs naevus tasks. Note a published corrigendum (PMID 28658222), not a retraction.

authors: Haenssle HA, Fink C, Schneiderbauer R et al.
title: Man against machine: diagnostic performance of a deep learning convolutional neural network for dermoscopic melanoma recognition in comparison to 58 dermatologists.
journal: Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology
takeaway: CNN vs 58 dermatologists on dermoscopic melanoma recognition: at dermatologists' sensitivity (86.6%), CNN specificity 82.5% vs 71.3%; CNN AUC 0.86 vs mean dermatologist 0.79. Added clinical information modestly helped dermatologists.

authors: Tschandl P, Rosendahl C, Kittler H
title: The HAM10000 dataset, a large collection of multi-source dermatoscopic images of common pigmented skin lesions.
takeaway: HAM10000: 10,015 dermoscopic images, 7 diagnostic categories of pigmented lesions, >50% pathology-confirmed (rest follow-up, consensus or confocal); training set of ISIC 2018 and widely used benchmark.

authors: Tschandl P, Codella N, Akay BN et al.
title: Comparison of the accuracy of human readers versus machine-learning algorithms for pigmented skin lesion classification: an open, web-based, international, diagnostic study.
takeaway: 511 human readers vs 139 algorithms on 7-class pigmented lesions: algorithms made 2.01 more correct diagnoses on average; top 3 algorithms beat experts (25.43 vs 18.78 correct). Advantage shrank on out-of-distribution images (11.4% vs 3.6% human underperformance).

authors: Tschandl P, Rinner C, Apalla Z et al.
title: Human-computer collaboration for skin cancer recognition.
takeaway: Good-quality AI support improved diagnostic accuracy above either AI or physicians alone, with least experienced clinicians gaining most; multiclass probabilities beat content-based image retrieval; faulty AI misled clinicians at all expertise levels.

authors: Pacheco AGC, Lima GR, Salomão AS et al.
title: PAD-UFES-20: A skin lesion dataset composed of patient data and clinical images collected from smartphones.
takeaway: PAD-UFES-20: 2,298 smartphone clinical images of 1,641 lesions from 1,373 patients (Brazil) with up to 21 clinical metadata fields; 6 diagnoses, 58.4% biopsy-proven including all cancers.

authors: Liu X, Cruz Rivera S, Moher D et al.
title: Reporting guidelines for clinical trial reports for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the CONSORT-AI extension.
takeaway: CONSORT-AI: 14 AI-specific items added to CONSORT 2010 for trials of AI interventions (describe the AI, setting, input/output handling, human-AI interaction, error analysis).

authors: Rotemberg V, Kurtansky N, Betz-Stablein B et al.
title: A patient-centric dataset of images and metadata for identifying melanomas using clinical context.
takeaway: SIIM-ISIC 2020 dataset: 33,126 dermoscopic images from 2,056 patients (avg 16 lesions/patient), 584 (1.8%) confirmed melanomas, with patient identifiers enabling 'ugly duckling'/patient-context modelling.

authors: Groh M, Harris C, Soenksen L et al.
title: Evaluating Deep Neural Networks Trained on Clinical Images in Dermatology with the Fitzpatrick 17k Dataset
journal: 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
takeaway: Fitzpatrick 17k: clinical-image dataset annotated with Fitzpatrick skin type, used to evaluate how training skin-type composition affects DNN accuracy across skin types (details not verified from abstract).

authors: Wen D, Khan SM, Ji Xu A et al.
title: Characteristics of publicly available skin cancer image datasets: a systematic review.
takeaway: Review of 21 public skin image datasets: of datasets reporting origin, 79% came only from Europe/North America/Oceania; ethnicity available for 1.3% of images and Fitzpatrick type for 2.1%; darker skin substantially under-represented.

authors: Combalia M, Codella N, Rotemberg V et al.
title: Validation of artificial intelligence prediction models for skin cancer diagnosis using dermoscopy images: the 2019 International Skin Imaging Collaboration Grand Challenge.
takeaway: ISIC 2019 challenge with an out-of-distribution class: algorithms beat experts in most categories but were far worse on unseen categories (6% vs 26% correct); top-25 algorithms called 47.1% of OOD images malignant. Artefacts (hair, pen marks) and source institution reduced accuracy.

authors: Daneshjou R, Barata C, Betz-Stablein B et al.
title: Checklist for Evaluation of Image-Based Artificial Intelligence Reports in Dermatology: CLEAR Derm Consensus Guidelines From the International Skin Imaging Collaboration Artificial Intelligence Working Group.
takeaway: CLEAR Derm: ISIC AI working group (19 experts) consensus checklist for developing and evaluating image-based dermatology AI (data, technique, technical assessment, application), targeting fairness, reliability and safety.

authors: Menzies SW, Sinz C, Menzies M et al.
title: Comparison of humans versus mobile phone-powered artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and management of pigmented skin cancer in secondary care: a multicentre, prospective, diagnostic, clinical trial.
takeaway: Prospective real-world mobile-phone AI in specialist settings: ISIC-derived algorithm significantly inferior to specialists (-11.6%) though superior to novices; AI management decisions inferior to specialists. Experimental superiority did not transfer to clinical practice.

authors: Hernández-Pérez C, Combalia M, Podlipnik S et al.
title: BCN20000: Dermoscopic Lesions in the Wild.
takeaway: BCN20000: 18,946 dermoscopic images (Hospital Clinic Barcelona, 2010-2016) including hard sites (nails, mucosa), large and hypopigmented lesions; 8 classes plus an out-of-distribution test class to emulate real practice.

authors: Papachristou P, Söderholm M, Pallon J et al.
title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based decision support for the detection of cutaneous melanoma in primary care: a prospective real-life clinical trial.
takeaway: Prospective Swedish primary-care study of a smartphone dermoscopy AI decision-support app: 253 lesions, 21 melanomas; AUROC 0.960 (max sensitivity 95.2%, specificity 84.5%); invasive melanoma AUROC 0.988. Small melanoma count.

authors: Marsden H, Kemos P, Venzi M et al.
title: Accuracy of an artificial intelligence as a medical device as part of a UK-based skin cancer teledermatology service.
takeaway: Skin Analytics DERM AI-as-a-medical-device within a UK teledermatology pathway: 789 lesions (67 malignant, 8 melanoma); at 91-92.5% sensitivity, DERM identified significantly more lesions not needing biopsy/urgent referral than teledermatologists (p=0.001). Only 4.0% of participants were Fitzpatrick IV-VI. (UKCA Class III status not stated in abstract.)

authors: Groh M, Badri O, Daneshjou R et al.
title: Deep learning-aided decision support for diagnosis of skin disease across skin tones.
takeaway: 389 dermatologists and 459 primary-care physicians across 39 countries: accuracy 38% vs 19%, both ~4 points worse on dark skin; fair DL decision support improved accuracy >33% but widened the generalists' skin-tone gap - overall accuracy gains do not guarantee reduced bias.

authors: Kim C, Gadgil SU, DeGrave AJ et al.
title: Transparent medical image AI via an image-text foundation model grounded in medical literature.
takeaway: MONET: CLIP-style image-text model trained on 105,550 dermatology images paired with literature text; densely scores clinical concepts (e.g., 'erythema', 'ulceration') competitively with supervised concept models, enabling dataset/model auditing and interpretable models.

authors: Zhou J, He X, Sun L et al.
title: Pre-trained multimodal large language model enhances dermatological diagnosis using SkinGPT-4.
takeaway: SkinGPT-4: vision transformer aligned with Llama-2-13b-chat on 52,929 skin images for interactive diagnosis and explanation; evaluated qualitatively/quantitatively on only 150 real-life cases with dermatologists.

authors: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P et al.
title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods.
takeaway: TRIPOD+AI: 27-item checklist (plus abstract checklist) for reporting prediction-model development/evaluation using regression or machine learning; supersedes TRIPOD 2015.

authors: Yan S, Yu Z, Primiero C et al.
title: A multimodal vision foundation model for clinical dermatology.
takeaway: PanDerm: multimodal vision foundation model (self-supervised pretraining across dermatology imaging modalities) evaluated on 28 benchmarks; state-of-the-art often with 10% of labels; beat clinicians by 10.2% in early melanoma detection from longitudinal images and improved clinician accuracy by 11% (dermoscopy) and non-dermatologists' differential by 16.5%.

authors: Wang L, Jacques SL, Zheng L
title: MCML--Monte Carlo modeling of light transport in multi-layered tissues
journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
takeaway: MCML: public-domain ANSI-C Monte Carlo code for steady-state photon transport in multi-layered tissue (in public domain since 1992), verified against other theories. It is the reference forward model used to generate training spectra for chromophore-inversion networks (e.g., Livecchi 2024) and validates faster diffusion approximations.

authors: Tsumura N, Haneishi H, Miyake Y
title: Independent-component analysis of skin color image
journal: Journal of the Optical Society of America. A, Optics, image science, and vision
takeaway: Separates melanin and hemoglobin maps from an ordinary RGB skin image via independent component analysis (ICA: blind separation of statistically independent sources) in optical-density space, assuming two spatially independent pigments and linearity. Results 'agree well with physiological knowledge' (qualitative); the foundation of most RGB-camera chromophore features.

authors: Jensen H, Marschner S, Levoy M, et al.
title: A practical model for subsurface light transport
journal: Proceedings of the 28th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques
takeaway: Seminal SIGGRAPH paper introducing the dipole diffusion approximation of the BSSRDF (bidirectional surface-scattering reflectance distribution function: how light entering at one point exits at another), making subsurface scattering in translucent media such as skin practical to render. Abstract not available via the tools used; content summarized from title/metadata and its role as the base model extended by the multipole/layered works below.

authors: Moncrieff M, Cotton S, Claridge E, et al.
title: Spectrophotometric intracutaneous analysis: a new technique for imaging pigmented skin lesions
takeaway: First clinical report of SIAscopy (8 narrow-band images, 400-1000 nm, 24x24 mm) deriving melanin, collagen and hemoglobin maps. In 348 lesions (52 melanomas), features such as dermal melanin, collagen holes and erythematous blush were reported as 80.1% specific and 82.7% sensitive (note the abstract assigns these numbers inversely to Claridge 2003 for the same dataset).

authors: Tsumura N, Ojima N, Sato K, et al.
title: Image-based skin color and texture analysis/synthesis by extracting hemoglobin and melanin information in the skin
takeaway: Adds shading removal (inverse lighting) to the ICA melanin/hemoglobin decomposition and validates physiologically with UV-B tanning and methyl-nicotinate erythema on arms; synthesizes tanning, alcohol flush and aging texture changes. Shows chromophore maps from consumer images respond to known physiological perturbations, but validation is visual comparison.

authors: Claridge E, Cotton S, Hall P, et al.
title: From colour to tissue histology: Physics-based interpretation of images of pigmented skin lesions
takeaway: Physics-based model of skin colouration maps each pixel to dermal/epidermal melanin, blood and collagen ('parametric maps'). In 348 pigmented lesions imaged with SIAscope, dermal melanin, abnormal blood distribution and size were most informative; classification gave 80.1% sensitivity and 82.7% specificity for melanoma. The clearest link between forward light-transport models and diagnostic features.

authors: Krishnaswamy A, Baranoski G
title: A Biophysically‐Based Spectral Model of Light Interaction with Human Skin
takeaway: BioSpec: a Monte Carlo, biophysically parameterized (pigment concentrations, layer thicknesses) model computing both spectral reflectance/transmittance and BSSRDF of skin, compared against measured skin data. The authors note applicability to spectral simulation of medical conditions, making it a template for physically grounded forward models.

authors: Donner C, Jensen H
title: Light diffusion in multi-layered translucent materials
takeaway: Extends the single dipole (valid only for semi-infinite homogeneous media) to a multipole model for thin slabs, with index-mismatch and rough-surface handling; layers are combined by convolving per-slab diffusion profiles plus a frequency-space Kubelka-Munk variant. Enables epidermis/dermis-style layered skin rendering; validation is visual/qualitative, not clinical.

authors: Donner C, Weyrich T, d'Eon E, et al.
title: A layered, heterogeneous reflectance model for acquiring and rendering human skin
takeaway: Spectral layered skin model with per-pixel spatially varying absorption/scattering and a thin absorbing interlayer, inverted from multispectral photographs using known chromophore spectra (inverse rendering) to recover per-pixel melanin/hemoglobin-type parameters. Reproduces freckles, veins, rashes and pressure-induced blood changes; reports 'low residual error' qualitatively, no clinical evaluation.

authors: Glud M, Gniadecki R, Drzewiecki KT
title: Spectrophotometric intracutaneous analysis versus dermoscopy for the diagnosis of pigmented skin lesions: prospective, double-blind study in a secondary reference centre
takeaway: Prospective double-blind comparison in 83 lesions (12 melanomas): SIAscopy sensitivity 100% vs dermoscopy 92%, but specificity 59% vs 81%. Independent evidence that chromophore-map devices did not outperform expert dermoscopy; an important caution on the clinical value of physics-derived features.

authors: Jacques SL
title: Optical properties of biological tissues: a review
takeaway: Canonical compilation of wavelength-dependent tissue absorption and scattering, with formulae to generate optical properties of generic tissue from blood, water, melanin, fat and small/large-scale scatterer fractions. Standard parameter source for any skin forward model; note a corrigendum exists (10.1088/0031-9155/58/14/5007, located via CrossRef, not read).

authors: Spigulis J, Oshina I
title: Snapshot RGB mapping of skin melanin and hemoglobin
takeaway: Snapshot chromophore mapping: three laser lines (473/532/659 nm) captured in one RGB frame are converted into melanin, oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin maps. Feasibility only; clinical performance discussed but not quantified in the abstract.

authors: Iglesias‐Guitian J, Aliaga C, Jarabo A, et al.
title: A Biophysically‐Based Model of the Optical Properties of Skin Aging
takeaway: Time-varying multi-layer biophysical model of skin optical properties under aging (structure and chromophore changes), parameterized by age, gender and skin type and drawing on tissue optics literature. Authors explicitly provide a simplified version 'valid for non-diagnostic applications', marking the boundary of graphics models.

authors: Gitlina Y, Guarnera G, Dhillon D, et al.
title: Practical Measurement and Reconstruction of Spectral Skin Reflectance
takeaway: Two practical spectral measurement protocols (complementary multispectral LED-sphere illumination; and a handheld Antera 3D dermatology camera) drive a spectral BSSRDF and estimate melanin, hemoglobin, melanin blend type and epidermal hemoglobin fraction, with a neural parameter estimator faster than lookup tables. Bridges a clinical skin-imaging device and graphics appearance reconstruction.

authors: Kuzmina I, Oshina I, Dambite L, et al.
title: Skin chromophore mapping by smartphone RGB camera under spectral band and spectral line illumination
takeaway: Smartphone RGB camera with LED-band vs laser-line illuminators on five benign neoplasm types, using Beer-Lambert inversion. Laser-line data gave ~10x higher oxyhemoglobin increases in vascular lesions; treating LED bands as single peak wavelengths can cause clinical misinterpretation. Shows that chromophore estimates depend heavily on illumination assumptions.

authors: Aliaga C, Xia M, Xie X, et al.
title: A Hyperspectral Space of Skin Tones for Inverse Rendering of Biophysical Skin Properties
takeaway: Builds a synthetic hyperspectral skin-tone space from a biophysical layered model plus Monte Carlo transport and learns an encoder-decoder inverse from RGB or spectral reflectance (to 1 um) to skin parameters. Reports high spectral similarity to the largest real skin spectral datasets with expanded gamut; deliberately exceeds medical parameter ranges, so recovered values are not clinically calibrated.

authors: Livecchi TT, Jacques SL, Subhash HM, et al.
title: Hyperspectral imaging with deep learning for quantification of tissue hemoglobin, melanin, and scattering
takeaway: Trains a neural network on 24,000 multi-layer Monte Carlo simulated reflectance spectra to invert hyperspectral images (205 bands, 420-830 nm) into hemoglobin, melanin and scattering maps, more than 4000x faster than iterative least squares, with low RMSE on 6000 simulated test spectra. In vivo demonstrations were finger occlusion and gingiva, not skin lesions; a template for simulation-trained physiological feature extraction.

authors: Wang Q, Luan F, Dai Y, et al.
title: A Biophysical-Based Skin Model for Heterogeneous Volume Rendering
takeaway: Recent biophysically based skin model for heterogeneous volume rendering (title/metadata only; abstract not retrievable). Indicates the 2025 graphics trend from diffusion profiles to heterogeneous volumetric skin with chromophore parameterization.

authors: Debevec P, Hawkins T, Tchou C, et al.
title: Acquiring the reflectance field of a human face
journal: Proceedings of the 27th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques  - SIGGRAPH '00
takeaway: Light Stage paper acquiring the reflectance field of a human face under dense controlled illumination for relighting, and estimating skin reflectance parameters. Abstract not retrievable via the tools used; summary from title/metadata.

authors: Weyrich T, Matusik W, Pfister H, et al.
title: Analysis of human faces using a measurement-based skin reflectance model
takeaway: Measured 3D geometry, skin reflectance and subsurface scattering in 149 subjects of varying age, gender and race; fit a model of spatially varying analytic BRDF, diffuse albedo and subsurface scattering. Parameter statistics varied by age, gender, skin type and external factors (sweat, cold, makeup) and were released publicly; moles/freckles are added only by texture synthesis.

authors: Ghosh A, Hawkins T, Peers P, et al.
title: Practical modeling and acquisition of layered facial reflectance
takeaway: Estimates layered facial reflectance (specular, single scattering, shallow and deep subsurface scattering) from 20 photographs using polarization-difference imaging and direct-indirect separation. Polarization separation is the same principle as cross-polarized dermoscopy, making this relevant to simulating imaging modality differences.

authors: Graham P, Tunwattanapong B, Busch J, et al.
title: Measurement‐Based Synthesis of Facial Microgeometry
takeaway: Synthesizes microstructure-level facial geometry by transferring detail from high-resolution scanned exemplar skin patches (polarization-based acquisition) onto mesostructure scans, and characterizes specular lobes at micro scale. Shows skin microrelief controls specular appearance; synthesis is exemplar-based texture transfer, not a model of lesional or disease topography.

authors: Sohaib A, Farooq AR, Atkinson GA, et al.
title: In vivo measurement of skin microrelief using photometric stereo in the presence of interreflections
journal: Journal of the Optical Society of America. A, Optics, image science, and vision
takeaway: Photometric stereo (shape from multiple illumination directions) using red/green/blue lights to correct interreflections for in vivo 3D skin microrelief, tested on Caucasian, Asian and African American subjects with reported improved reconstruction. Notes that non-diffuse, wavelength-dependent skin BRDF affects recovered topography, a pitfall when inferring texture from photographs.

authors: Linming F, Wei H, Anqi L, et al.
title: Comparison of two skin imaging analysis instruments: The VISIA® from Canfield vs the ANTERA 3D® CS from Miravex
journal: Skin research and technology : official journal of International Society for Bioengineering and the Skin (ISBS) [and] International Society for Digital Imaging of Skin (ISDIS) [and] International Society for Skin Imaging (ISSI)
takeaway: In 28 subjects, Antera 3D (multidirectional multi-wavelength LED illumination) wrinkle, texture, melanin, hemoglobin and pore metrics correlated with age; VISIA red area strongly correlated with Antera hemoglobin, and texture values correlated across devices, but wrinkle and pore measures did not. Device-specific topography/colour indices are not interchangeable.

authors: Ghorbani A, Natarajan V, Coz D, et al.
title: DermGAN: Synthetic Generation of Clinical Skin Images with Pathology
takeaway: DermGAN adapts Pix2Pix to synthesize clinical skin-condition images with controllable lesion size, location and underlying skin colour; dermatologists in a Turing-style test judged images similar to real and condition-consistent. As augmentation, overall classifier performance was comparable to baseline while improving rare malignant conditions.

authors: Bissoto A, Valle E, Avila S
title: GAN-Based Data Augmentation and Anonymization for Skin-Lesion Analysis: A Critical Review
journal: 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
takeaway: Carefully designed experiments show GAN-based augmentation for skin-lesion diagnosis yields favorable results only on out-of-distribution test sets, and GAN-based anonymization (replacing real images) likewise. Authors urge caution adopting GANs in medical applications given costs and risks.

authors: Rezk E, Eltorki M, El-Dakhakhni W
title: Improving Skin Color Diversity in Cancer Detection: Deep Learning Approach
takeaway: Style transfer generated darker-skin versions of lesion images; 62.2% of votes judged generated images real and eight dermatologists diagnosed them correctly at 0.75. Adding generated images raised CNN accuracy from 0.56 to 0.76 and AUC from 0.63 to 0.72. Small test regime; transformed skin tone may not reproduce how lesions actually present on darker skin.

authors: Sagers LW, Diao JA, Groh M, et al.
title: Improving dermatology classifiers across populations using images generated by large diffusion models
takeaway: DALL-E 2 generated photorealistic skin disease images across skin types; augmenting Fitzpatrick 17k training data improved classification overall and especially for underrepresented groups. Proprietary generator; no numbers in abstract.

authors: Sinha A, Kawahara J, Pakzad A, et al.
title: DermSynth3D: Synthesis of in-the-wild annotated dermatology images
takeaway: DermSynth3D blends skin-disease patterns onto 3D textured human meshes with a differentiable renderer, rendering 2D images under chosen viewpoints, lighting and backgrounds, with dense labels (skin/lesion segmentation, body part, boxes, depth, camera/light). Models trained on synthetic data were evaluated on real dermatology images; open code. Lesion appearance is pasted texture, not physically simulated.

authors: Kim A, Saharkhiz N, Sizikova E, et al.
title: S-SYNTH: Knowledge-Based, Synthetic Generation of Skin Images
takeaway: FDA S-SYNTH: open-source knowledge-based simulator with an anatomically inspired multi-layer, multi-component skin and growing-lesion model, controlling skin colour, hair, lesion shape and blood fraction. Segmentation results on synthetic data followed similar comparative trends as real dermatologic images, positioning synthetic data for controlled AI evaluation (abstract retrieved via arXiv preprint).

authors: Ktena I, Wiles O, Albuquerque I, et al.
title: Generative models improve fairness of medical classifiers under distribution shifts
takeaway: Diffusion models learn label-efficient augmentations; adding synthetic samples improved robustness in histopathology, chest X-ray and dermatology and improved fairness by raising diagnostic accuracy in underrepresented groups, especially out of distribution. Highest-profile evidence that generative augmentation can help subgroup performance; effect sizes not stated in the abstract.

authors: Akrout M, Gyepesi B, Holló P, et al.
title: Diffusion-Based Data Augmentation for Skin Disease Classification: Impact Across Original Medical Datasets to Fully Synthetic Images
takeaway: Text-prompt-controlled diffusion augmentation of a macroscopic skin disease dataset; a classifier trained on a fully synthetic dataset maintained similar accuracy to the real-data classifier. Shows synthetic data can substitute but not clearly exceed real data; no fairness breakdown in abstract.

authors: Farooq MA, Yao W, Schukat M, et al.
title: Derm-T2IM: Harnessing Synthetic Skin Lesion Data via Stable Diffusion Models for Enhanced Skin Disease Classification using ViT and CNN
journal: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Annual International Conference
takeaway: Few-shot fine-tuned Stable Diffusion generates dermatoscopic lesion images (Derm-T2IM) that improved robustness of CNN and ViT classifiers on several real-world skin cancer datasets; data and model open-sourced. No numeric results in the abstract.

authors: Izu-Belloso RM, Ibarrola-Altuna R, Rodriguez-Alonso A
title: Generative Adversarial Networks in Dermatology: A Narrative Review of Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
takeaway: Reviews 27 GAN studies in dermatology across 11 use cases (under-represented phenotype synthesis, segmentation, denoising, super-resolution, colour standardization) and evaluation metrics (FID, SSIM, IS, Dice). Concludes few GAN models have reached clinical integration and calls for standardized protocols and clinical validation.

authors: Sizikova E, Saharkhiz N, Kim A, et al.
title: Synthetic skin image generation using a physics-based, object-to-image computational pipeline
journal: International journal of computer assisted radiology and surgery
takeaway: Extended S-SYNTH evaluation: synthetic data reproduce comparative trends of patient images for lesion segmentation and S-SYNTH images can enhance diffusion-model performance. Emphasizes tight control of parameter space and creation of rare examples/annotations missing from patient data.

authors: D'Alessandro B, Dhawan AP
title: 3-D volume reconstruction of skin lesions for melanin and blood volume estimation and lesion severity analysis
study_type: method paper with small clinical validation
takeaway: Inverse reconstruction of melanin and blood layer volumes beneath lesions from multispectral transillumination images, using a genetic algorithm with voxel-based Monte Carlo as forward model. On 14 clinical lesions, average blood-layer thickness and blood/lesion volume ratio separated mild vs moderate/severe with 100% accuracy (very small sample).

authors: Betz-Stablein B, D'Alessandro B, Koh U, et al.
title: Reproducible Naevus Counts Using 3D Total Body Photography and Convolutional Neural Networks
takeaway: CNN on 3D TBP for naevus counting (train 57,742 lesions/82 subjects; test 4,868/10): lesion-level sensitivity 79% and specificity 91% for lesions >=2 mm, kappa 0.56 (moderate), rising to kappa 0.72 for >=5 mm; agreement lower with many seborrhoeic keratoses.

authors: Kurtansky NR, D'Alessandro BM, Gillis MC, et al.
title: The SLICE-3D dataset: 400,000 skin lesion image crops extracted from 3D TBP for skin cancer detection
takeaway: SLICE-3D: >400,000 lesion crops from 3D total-body photographs across seven centers, comparable in optical resolution to smartphone images, intended for triage-grade (non-dermoscopic) detection (basis of the ISIC 2024 challenge). Key real-data counterpart for any synthetic/rendered lesion pipeline.

authors: Akbarialiabad H, Pasdar A, Murrell DF
title: Digital twins in dermatology, current status, and the road ahead
takeaway: Searched five databases to Feb 2024 and found no direct studies applying digital twins in dermatology; frames concept, barriers (disease complexity, privacy, specialized algorithms). Establishes that 'skin digital twin' is aspirational as of 2024.

authors: Primiero CA, Janda M, Soyer HP
title: Skin 2.0: How Cutaneous Digital Twins Could Reshape Dermatology
takeaway: Perspective from the Brisbane 3D-TBP group on 'cutaneous digital twins' integrating serial total-body imaging with other data. No abstract available; included for framing only.

authors: Saha A, Adeola J, Ferrera N, et al.
title: Skin region images extracted from 3D total body photographs for lesion detection
takeaway: iToBoS dataset: 16,954 skin-region images (~7x9 cm) from 100 participants captured with 3D TBP, with bounding boxes for suspicious lesions plus anatomical site, age group and sun-damage score. Provides context-rich (non-centred) real images for detection benchmarking.

authors: Huang WL, Xue M, Liu Z, et al.
title: Revisiting lesion tracking in 3D total body photography
takeaway: Lesion tracking between pairs of 3D textured total-body meshes via template correspondence and flow-field refinement; introduces 25K annotated lesion pairs across 198 subjects. Success rate 90.1% at 10 mm and 98.1% matching accuracy for subjects with >200 lesions; enables longitudinal change detection, the core clinical use of 3D reconstruction.
